full_judgment:
A.M. Mahmudur Rahman, J. :- By this Rule the opposite party No. 1 was called upon to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 21.9.1983 of the learned Sub-Judge, Jhalakati made in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 112 of 1982 upholding the order of detention of the petitioners and two others in Civil prison passed by the learned Munsif, Jhalakati on 16.6.82 in Miscellaneous case No. 104 of 1978 should not be set aside. 

 The opposite party No. 1 filed an application under Sub-Rule 3 of Rule 2 of Order 39 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for violation of an injunction order passed on 8.4.78 by the learned Munsif upon an application filed by the opposite party No. 1 under Rule 1 of Order 39 of the Code in connection with Title Suit No. 99 of 78 instituted by the opposite party No.1 against the petitioners and others. By the said order dated 8.4.1978 the petitioner were restrained from entering into the land in suit and changing the character and nature of the same. The opposite party No. 1 alleged in the said application under sub-rule (3) of Rule 2 of Order 39 that the petitioners along with large number of people intentionally and willfully cut earth on 30.4.78 from the disputed land causing loss of Tk. 50,000/- to him although they were restrained from doing so by the aforesaid order of injunction. The miscellaneous case No. 104 of 1978 was stated by the Ld. Munsif upon the said application. The said case was resisted by the petitioner No.1 by filing a written objection. He denied the material allegations made in the aforesaid application contending that no notice of injunction was served upon them. He also filed an affidavit wherein a statement was made to the effect that cutting of earth from the suit land was done before filing of the aforesaid suit and they did not cut any earth from the suit land after the order of injunction was passed and denied allegation of violating the injunction order. The opposite party No 1 also filed an application in the said case praying for local inspection to ascertain whether earth was cut as alleged and the learned Munsif appointed an Advocate Commissioner for the purpose. And the Advocate Commissioner after holding local inspection submitted a report. The petitioner No. 1 filed objection against the said report but the court rejected the objection and accepted the report. The petitioners against the order of acceptance of the report went upto High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision case No. 926 of 1978, The Rule, however was discharged on contest on 13.11.1979. 

 1.	Is the Misc. Case maintainable in the present form ? 

 4. The learned Munsif on consideration of the evidence on record held that the petitioners and two others intentionally violated the injunction order passed on 8.4.78 and passed an order for detention of the petitioners and 2 others in Civil prison for two weeks with a direction upon the opposite-party to deposit Tk. 500/- in the court as a maintenance allowance. As against the aforesaid order the petitioners preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 112 of 1982 before the learned District Judge. The said appeal, on transfer, was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, Jhalakati, who, however, concurred with the finding of the learned Munsif and dismissed the appeal upholding the order of detention. 

 5. The learned Advocate for the petitioners firstly, submitted that the proceeding under sub-rule (3) of Rule 2 of Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure is a quasi-criminal proceeding and the petitioners were prejudiced in the trial as the trial Court followed a wrong procedure in deciding the Miscellaneous case. Secondly, he submitted that the learned Munsif made a wrong approach in deciding the case by starting discussion of the evidence of the witness of the petitioners at first against whom the allegation for violation of the order of the court was made and wrongly shifted the onus on the petitioners to prove their innocence. 

 6. The learned Advocate for the petitioners very strenuously urged that the procedure followed by the learned Munsif in deciding the Miscellaneous case was wrong. He submitted that the proceeding initiated upon an application under sub-rule 3 of Rule 2 of Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure is a quasi-criminal in nature and the person against whom the allegation as to violation of the court's order was brought should have been confronted with a charge or issue disclosing exact, definite and precise allegations so that he can understand the extent and nature of the allegations without any ambiguity whatsoever. But in the present case he submitted no such allegation finds place in the point and/ or charge framed by the trial court while framing the issue in this respect. He referred to me relevant issue No. 3 as quoted above framed by the Learned trial court in this respect & argued that the said point is vague and does not at all disclose the particulars of the offence alleged against and as such the petitioners were prejudiced in the trial of their case as they were not in a position to explain away the allegation brought against them. The Id Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 on the other hand, submitted that as the petitioners led evidence in support of their case they were not misled by framing such issue or point and were not at all prejudiced in their trial. 

 7. In support of This contention Learned vacate for the petitioners referred me to the case of Halim Vs. Shah Din reported in PLD 1953 (Lah) 77 That case also arose out of an application under sub-rule 3 of Rule 2 of Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure for violation of an injunction order granted by the court. In delivering the judgment of the report A.R Cornelius, A.C.J. (as his Lordship was then) observed. 

 "It is true that the present case lies in the civil Jurisdiction, but penalties involved are clearly of a criminal nature, and, notwithstanding that no precise procedure has been laid down, it is expected that any Court which feels called upon to impose these penalties should proceed as nearly as possible in the same manner as a criminal Court would proceed; in other words, that at the earliest opportunity, when it has formed the opinion that facts exist which may require the imposition of the penalties, the Court shall put the person at fault on his guard by framing a question or an issue which should embody all the elements of a charge under the criminal jurisdiction". 

 He also relied on the decision in the case of Momtaz Afeah-Vs-Musammat Amirunnessa reported in 9 D.L.R 444. 

 "That case also arose out of an application under sub rule 3 of Rule 2 Order 39 of the Code for violation of an order of injunction. In the judgment of the report his Lordship Rahman, J (as his Lordship was then) observed as follows:- 

 8. Now, let us see whether the point formulated by the learned Munsif embody all the elements of a charge under the criminal jurisdiction as has been laid down in the case of Halim Vs. Shah Din The relevant issue framed the learned Munsif is point No. 2 is in the following terms 2. Have the O.Ps intentionally violated the order of the court? From reading the said point (issue) it is difficult on our part to understand as to on what date in respect of which matter and in respect of which order of the court the petitioners committed the alleged offence as said to have been committed in terms of the said point No. 2 as formulated by the learned Munsif. The point does not at all disclose or indicate with exactness the allegations brought against the petitioners rather it was framed in a vague and general way. This type of framing of issue in a vague and general way in deciding a case in a proceeding under sub-rule 3 of Rule 2 of Order 29 of the Civil Procedure Code for the purpose of finding the guilt of the alleged offenders cannot be said to be permissible in law. In a proceeding initiated upon an application under Sub-Rule 3 of Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure bringing allegation for violation of an injunction order passed by a court against the offenders the trial court must frame the issue in such a manner so that all the elements of a charge under criminal jurisdiction find place in the issue so that the persons against whom the allegation of violation of Court's order is brought is in way misled by such issue and is prejudiced in their trial. In this case, the point No. 2 as has been framed by the learned trial court does not at all indicate the time, manner, place & the order in respect of which the violation as alleged said to have been committed by the petitioners. Although the proceeding is under civil jurisdiction yet the allegation against the offenders being of grave nature calling for, if proved, a serious penalties and the proceeding being quasi-criminal in nature the court is called upon to frame issue on the allegation disclosing all the material particulars and ingredients constituting the offence so that the alleged offenders are not mislead by such issue and are not prejudiced in the trial. But in this case this procedure has not been followed by the trial court resulting miscarriage of justice. This aspect of the case at all did not receive due consideration of the Lower Appellate Court which equally committed an error in maintaining the order of detention. 

 "Firstly I shall discuss the evidence of the OP to see whether the O.Ps have violated the injunction order. In proving his case the OPI has examined four witnesses including himself as O.P.W 1" and he further observed :- 

 "The OPI examined only those three interested witness in the cases but he could bring some independent witness to say that did not cut earth on 30-4-78". 

 As, being of the opinion that the proceeding initiated in this case is a quasi-criminal proceeding and the point No. 2 formulated way not framed properly and correctly, I send back the case to the trial court. I am not inclined to embark upon discussion on other points raised by the learned Advocates. 

 11. For the reason stated above, I hold that the petitioners were misled by point No. 2 and were prejudiced in their trial as they were not confronted with all the elements of charge embodying in the said point and were not in a petition to adduce evidence to explain away the circumstances standing against them which are wanting in this case. In this view of the matter, I set aside the judgments and orders of the Courts below and I send back the Miscellaneous case No. 104 of 1978 on remand to the trial Court for disposal after framing proper issue on allegations in the light of the observation made above in this judgment.
